Jefferson Davis. A Mississippi plantation owner, U.S. Senator, and Secretary of War who became the first and only president of the Confederate States of America. He led the Confederacy through the Civil War from 1861 to 1865, defending the cause of Southern secession and slavery even as Confederate military resources dwindled. His rigid leadership and inability to adapt strategy contributed to the South's defeat, and he spent years in prison after the war as a symbol of the rebellion.

Born in Kentucky in 1808, Davis grew up in Mississippi and became a wealthy plantation owner with hundreds of enslaved laborers. He served as U.S. Secretary of War under President Franklin Pierce from 1853 to 1857, advocating for Southern expansion and slavery's extension. In February 1861, weeks before the fall of Fort Sumter, he was elected president of the Confederate States of America. That April, he ordered the bombardment of Fort Sumter, initiating the war's opening battle and the nation's bloodiest conflict. Throughout the war, Davis centralized Confederate power and pursued aggressive war aims, clashing with generals and state leaders over strategy and resources. After Robert E. Lee's surrender in 1865, Davis attempted to flee but was captured by Union forces and imprisoned for two years. His conflicts with Lee, whose military judgment often diverged from Davis's strategic vision, exemplified the tensions that weakened Confederate leadership during the war.
